title: Life Processes

steps.title: Maintenance never takes a break
steps.intro: Life processes keep organised living structures functioning, even during sleep. Visible movement alone cannot distinguish every living thing from a non-living object. The source’s virus example concerns the lack of independent metabolism outside host cells, not the absence of all physical molecular motion.
steps.simple: Nutrition supplies materials and energy sources; respiration makes energy available; transport distributes materials; excretion removes metabolic wastes.
example: Nutrition supplies materials and energy sources; respiration makes energy available; transport distributes materials; excretion removes metabolic wastes.
Invisible molecular activity continues in living cells. A stationary plant can be alive, and a moving car need not be.

steps.title: Build food from simple materials
steps.intro: Photosynthetic autotrophs use light captured by chlorophyll to make organic food from CO2 and water. They also need mineral nutrients.
steps.simple: A school overall equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, with light and chlorophyll. Released O2 originates from water.

steps.title: A pore has a gate
steps.intro: Stomata allow gas exchange while guard cells regulate opening and water loss. Gas exchange also occurs across other plant surfaces.
steps.simple: Water entering guard cells makes them turgid and tends to open the pore; water loss tends to close it.

steps.title: Different organisms obtain food differently
steps.intro: Heterotrophs obtain organic material made by other organisms. Their feeding structures reflect their food and environment.
steps.simple: Fungi such as bread mould digest externally and absorb products; parasites such as Cuscuta, ticks, lice, leeches and tapeworms obtain nutrients from hosts.

steps.intro: Gastric glands release HCl, pepsin and mucus. Muscular stomach walls mix food and a sphincter regulates release to the small intestine.
steps.simple: HCl provides the acidic conditions for pepsin and helps kill many swallowed microbes. Pepsin digests proteins.

steps.title: Bile helps enzymes reach fat
steps.intro: The small intestine receives bile from the liver and pancreatic juices. Digestion finishes here before nutrients are absorbed.
steps.simple: Bile helps neutralise acidic contents and emulsifies large fat globules into smaller droplets; bile is not a lipase. Pancreatic bicarbonate also helps provide suitable pH.

steps.intro: Numerous thin-walled villi increase the small intestine’s absorption area. Blood vessels take up many soluble nutrients; lymphatic lacteals carry much absorbed fat.
steps.simple: Small intestine length and diet differ among animals; herbivore digestion often depends on microbial partners for cellulose. Humans do not digest cellulose with their own enzymes.

steps.title: One first step, several later routes
steps.intro: Glucose is split into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm. Later pathways depend on the organism and conditions.
steps.simple: With oxygen, mitochondrial reactions release CO2, water and more usable energy overall. Yeast fermentation yields ethanol and CO2 without oxygen.

steps.title: Transfer energy through ATP
steps.intro: Respiration releases energy that cells capture in ATP. ATP hydrolysis can be coupled to muscle contraction, synthesis and nerve activity.
steps.simple: ADP + phosphate can be used to make ATP; ATP hydrolysis yields ADP and phosphate and can drive cellular work.
example: ADP + phosphate can be used to make ATP; ATP hydrolysis yields ADP and phosphate and can drive cellular work.

The source’s roughly 30.5 kJ/mol is a standard biochemical free-energy value, not an identical fixed release in every cell. Breaking an isolated bond itself requires energy; the overall hydrolysis reaction releases usable free energy.

steps.title: Plants respire in daylight too
steps.intro: Plants respire continuously. Net gas exchange depends on photosynthesis, respiration and environmental conditions.
steps.simple: At night without photosynthesis, respiration generally gives net O2 uptake and CO2 release.

steps.title: Move air to a protected surface
steps.intro: Air travels through nose, airway, bronchi and branching bronchioles to alveoli. Hairs, mucus and cilia help protect the respiratory passages.
steps.simple: Cartilage supports the trachea. On inhalation ribs rise and the diaphragm contracts/flattens, increasing chest volume and lowering pressure so air enters.
example: Cartilage supports the trachea. On inhalation ribs rise and the diaphragm contracts/flattens, increasing chest volume and lowering pressure so air enters.

steps.title: Exchange across a thin, moist wall
steps.intro: Many alveoli provide a large surface, a short diffusion distance and an extensive capillary network. Ventilation and blood flow maintain gradients.
steps.simple: O2 moves from alveolar air into blood; CO2 moves from blood into alveoli under the usual gradients.
example: O2 moves from alveolar air into blood; CO2 moves from blood into alveoli under the usual gradients.
The book’s roughly 80 m² is an illustrative estimate; area varies. Haemoglobin in red cells carries most O2; most CO2 travels as bicarbonate in blood, with some dissolved and some bound.

steps.title: Follow a complete double circuit
steps.intro: Blood passes through the heart twice in a full lung-and-body circuit. Valves promote one-way flow.
steps.simple: Body → venae cavae → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.
example: Body → venae cavae → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.
Atria receive blood; ventricles pump it onward and have thicker walls. The left ventricle pumps through the systemic circuit. Arteries lead away from the heart, not necessarily oxygen-rich.

steps.intro: Four-chambered mammal and bird hearts separate oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor streams, supporting high metabolism and body-temperature regulation.
steps.simple: Fish have a two-chambered heart and a single circulation: heart → gills → body → heart.
